extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, dramatists, and students of poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic (and epic) poetry and drama, focusing on plot, character, recognition, diction, and style according to classical poetics. Advice is aimed at constructing effective tragedies (and narrative epics) that produce pity and fear and respect formal unity and diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject selection: few houses / limited scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The best tragedies are founded on the story of a few houses, on the fortunes of a limited set of families or persons who have done or suffered something terrible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid recounting every legend in the same play; choose a small number of connected families whose histories contain moving, tragic incidents. This focus makes the play more tragic in effect on stage and in competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke pity and fear by plot structure not spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means; but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is the better way, and indicates a superior poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct incidents so that hearing the tale thrills and moves without needing visual spectacle. Avoid relying on monstrous spectacle or extraneous aids to produce tragic feeling; the proper pleasure of Tragedy comes from imitation that produces pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose actions between close relations to produce pity
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of tragic effect must happen between persons who are near or dear to one another (e.g., brother kills brother, son his father, mother her son).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents among enemies or indifferent persons rarely excite pity (except insofar as suffering itself is pitiful). Seek situations involving kinship, friendship, or close ties to maximize tragic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle traditional material with invention and skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may not destroy the framework of received legends but ought to show invention of his own and skilfully handle the traditional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work creatively with myths and traditions—preserve essential framework but introduce original touches and skilful reworking so the old material yields fresh tragic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred manner of terrible deeds (ranking of modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only certain possible ways a horrific deed may occur (done knowingly, done in ignorance with discovery afterwards, about to act and then not acting, about to act and discover before doing), and these are not equal in effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best: deed perpetrated in ignorance with discovery afterwards (startling, tragic). Next: deed actually perpetrated knowingly. Worst: intending to act knowingly and then not acting (shocking but not tragic because no disaster follows). Use examples (Medea, Oedipus, Antigone) to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: First and most important, character must be good: any speech or action that manifests moral purpose will be expressive of character and make the character good (relative to class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should have morally intelligible aims; even lower-status characters (women, slaves) can be 'good' relative to their type. Goodness of purpose helps make actions believable and sympathetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: propriety (fitness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second, character must show propriety: attributes and actions appropriate to the sex, rank, or type (e.g., manly valour belongs to men; valour in a woman may be inappropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match traits and behaviors to the character's class and role; avoid indecorous or inappropriate manifestations that break plausibility or offend expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: true to life
rubrics_metrics.description: Third, character must be true to life; this is distinct from goodness and propriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters in ways consistent with real human behavior and psychology; avoid caricature or implausible motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth, character must be consistent: even if the original or model is inconsistent, the portrayal must be consistently inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain internal coherence in how a character speaks and acts; sudden, motiveless degradations or shifts are faults (examples: Menelaus in Orestes, Iphigenia at Aulis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation: incidents must arise from the plot (avoid internal deus ex machina)
rubrics_metrics.description: The unravelling of the plot, no less than the complication, must arise out of the plot itself; the 'Deus ex Machina' should be employed only for events external to the drama, not for internal resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid irrational or externally imposed resolutions within the action. If something irrational must occur, place it outside the action proper and report or foretell it via the gods or other external devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ennoble types while preserving likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Tragedy imitates persons above the common level, the poet should reproduce likeness and yet make the characters more beautiful (ennoble types while keeping distinguishing traits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent defects (irascibility, indolence) faithfully but elevated; follow examples like Achilles' portrayal—preserve type but ennoble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition: prefer natural incident-driven recognitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions vary (by signs/tokens, poet-invented declarations, memory, reasoning, composite false inference), and of all recognitions the best is that which arises from the incidents themselves—natural discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid poverty-of-wit signs or contrived revelations (tokens, forced speeches where a character simply declares identity). Use recognitions that are natural to the situation or that follow from reasonable thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition: rank and pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition by signs or tokens is least artistic; recognition invented by the poet (character gratuitously announcing identity) is poor; reasoning or memory-based recognitions are better; natural incident-driven recognitions are best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing recognition devices, prefer those that avoid artificial proofs and produce startling but believable discovery; be cautious of formal proofs or arbitrary tokens that feel contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization and stage-situational awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing plot and diction, the poet should place the scene before his eyes, seeing everything vividly as if a spectator, to detect inconsistencies and what is in keeping with the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagine the physical staging and gestures; ensure stage facts (who is where, who exits/enters) are consistent—oversights in stage situation offend the audience (example: Carcinus' failure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gesture and delivery: appropriate embodiment of emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Work out the play with appropriate gestures; those who feel emotion are most convincing through natural sympathy: one who is agitated storms, one who is angry rages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan expressive physicality that matches emotional states; poetry implies either a natural gift or an inspired excess, but realistic gestures increase conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story planning: sketch outline then fill relevant episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the poet takes the story ready-made or constructs it, he should first sketch its general outline, and then fill in episodes and amplify in detail; episodes must be relevant to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a clear general plan (beginning/middle/end), then insert short episodes that extend or illustrate but remain tied to the main action (examples: Iphigenia, Odyssey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot structure: Complication and Unravelling (unity of action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts—Complication and Unravelling (Denouement). The Complication extends from the beginning to the turning-point; the Unravelling from the change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure identity of tragedy is judged by plot (complication + unravelling). Avoid multiplicity of plots; a tragedy should present a single action with unity—do not convert epic multiplicity into tragic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epic structure in tragedy (no multiplicity of plots)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make an Epic structure into a Tragedy—avoid multiplicity of plots and excessive scope that belong to epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a manageable portion of a larger story rather than attempting the whole war or tale; overcomplication by many incidents undermines stage success (examples: dramatising whole Iliad or Niobe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine core poetic elements where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should endeavor to combine all poetic elements (reversals, recognitions, scenes of suffering, diction, thought, song, spectacle) or at least the greatest and most important among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to include as many key elements as appropriate to enhance tragic effect; critics expect excellence across various poetic faculties, and a single poet now is expected to excel in multiple lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus integration: chorus as actor sharing the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole and share in the action (as in Sophocles) rather than serving as mere interludes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choral songs that pertain little to the subject; choral material should contribute to or participate in the dramatic action rather than acting as detached entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought: speech must produce rhetorical effects; incidents should speak for themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought includes every effect to be produced by speech—proof, refutation, excitation of feelings (pity, fear, anger), suggestion of importance, etc. Incidents should speak for themselves without verbal exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design speeches to produce intended effects while allowing incidents to convey their meaning directly. The speaker's words should produce thought-effects, not replace the incident's dramatic function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and Modes of Utterance: fit utterance to delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction involves modes of utterance (command, prayer, statement, threat, question) which belongs to the art of Delivery; knowing these forms is necessary though it falls to delivery specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure utterance types are appropriate to dramatic function and delivery; mistakes of mode are more about delivery but the poet should be aware of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style: clear without being mean; balance current and rare words; moderation in metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean. Clearness comes from current/proper words; loftiness comes from unusual words, metaphor, ornamental devices; but extremes create riddles or jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a measured mix of current and unusual words, metaphors, lengthenings/contractings for distinction while preserving perspicuity. Avoid overuse of rare terms or metaphors that make diction a riddle or jargon. Command of metaphor marks genius. Genre-specific guidance: compound words suit dithyrambs, rare words heroic poetry, metaphors iambic, and iambic should favor prose-like words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-formation and variation: tasteful use of coinages, lengthening, contraction, alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may be newly-coined, lengthened, contracted, or altered; such licenses can give distinction but require moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selective deviations from normal idiom (lengthening, contraction, altered forms) can elevate diction when used sparingly; critics who caricature these licenses err if they object to measured, skillful use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic poetry: choose single action/portion and appropriate metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry must, like tragedy, be constructed on dramatic principles and have a single action whole and complete with beginning, middle, end; it differs from tragedy in scale and metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to cover an entire vast subject in epic; detach a single portion and admit other events as episodes. Use appropriate metre and scale (Iliad and Odyssey exemplary) and preserve epic's distinctiveness from tragedy.
